title: Technological Obstacle - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Understand what constitutes a Technological Obstacle and how overcoming it supports your claim in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: A technological obstacle, in Canada's SR&ED program, is a technological uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic test, Canadian claimants must show they faced such uncertainty, tested hypotheses systematically and kept contemporaneous documentation to qualify for federal investment tax credits.

body.text: A technological obstacle, in Canada's SR&ED program, is a technological uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic test, Canadian claimants must show they faced such uncertainty, tested hypotheses systematically and kept contemporaneous documentation to qualify for federal investment tax credits.

This report provides a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program, provincial and territorial research and development (R&D) tax credits, direct federal innovation funding instruments, administrative filing protocols, and governing judicial precedents as of November 2026.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Parliament and the Department of Finance Canada enacted the most expansive overhaul of federal R&D tax incentives in four decades. Through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (superseding the interim $4,500,000 figure proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 35% enhanced credit to eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs), and reinstated both immediate Section 37 expensing and Section 127 ITC eligibility for SR&ED capital property and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024. Administrative delivery simultaneously shifted toward upfront certainty: on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process issuing technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks, while Budget 2026 (updated November 5, 2026) proposed expanding SR&ED eligibility to cover downstream commercialization expenses—specifically regulatory approvals/certifications and intellectual property (IP) protection—at a projected five-year fiscal cost of $930,000,000. Across the provinces, however, subnational harmonization has fractured: Québec replaced its legacy R&D credits with the refundable 30%/20% Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, and specialist Canadian R&D tax advisory analyses report that while British Columbia harmonized fully with the $6,000,000 federal framework and made its credit permanent, Saskatchewan adopted a targeted $2,000,000 refundable threshold and Ontario, Alberta, and Manitoba retained independent statutory limits.
1. Executive Legislative Audit and Macro-Fiscal Landscape (As of November 2026)
1.1 Historical Trajectory and the 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms

Federal income tax incentives for private-sector research in Canada originated in 1944 with the introduction of current expenditure deductibility under what is now Section 37 of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)). Tax credits for R&D first entered federal law in 1948, immediate deductibility for SR&ED capital expenditures followed in 1961, and the structural foundation of the modern two-tier SR&ED ITC regime was established between 1983 and 1985, reinforced by small-business policy enhancements in Budget 1996. Within the Department of Finance Canada's fiscal accounting architecture, SR&ED tax incentives are classified as non-structural tax measures (with the refundable credit component treated as a government transfer payment) designed to correct a classic market failure: because the technological knowledge generated by domestic R&D spills over to other firms and industrial sectors, private enterprises would underinvest relative to the socially optimal benchmark without public fiscal support.

From 2012 through late 2024, federal legislative policy narrowed the SR&ED expenditure base and lowered statutory credit rates. Budget 2012 enacted four major structural reductions: it lowered the general SR&ED ITC rate from 20% to 15% effective January 1, 2014; eliminated capital expenditures and capital lease outlays from both the Section 37 deduction pool and Section 127 ITC base for expenditures incurred after 2013; stepped down the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for notional overhead from 65% of directly engaged salaries and wages to 60% in 2013 and 55% in 2014 and subsequent years; and reduced arm's-length third-party contract inclusions to 80% effective January 1, 2013 to exclude assumed contractor profit margins. Apart from Budget 2019, which repealed prior-year taxable income as a factor in determining a Canadian-controlled private corporation's (CCPC's) annual expenditure limit for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019, federal caps remained static at $3,000,000 for more than a decade.
Beginning in December 2024, Parliament reversed those Budget 2012 contractions through a three-step legislative sequence that culminated in Royal Assent in March 2026:

items: 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and August 2025 Legislative Proposals: Tabled on December 16, 2024, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, raising the lower and upper prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, extending eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate to ECPCs, and reinstating immediate expensing and ITC eligibility for SR&ED capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (and qualifying lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024). Detailed draft legislative and regulatory proposals implementing these reforms were released by the Department of Finance Canada on August 15, 2025.

Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025): Tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025 (Canada Strong), Budget 2025 confirmed the FES 2024 and August 15, 2025 legislative package while modifying the enhanced credit cap—further increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from the previously announced $4,500,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Corporate tax auditors must note that secondary CPA blogs or outdated compliance guides still citing a $4,500,000 federal expenditure limit for 2025 or 2026 taxation years reflect superseded FES 2024 proposals rather than enacted federal law. The incremental Budget 2025 expansion to $6,000,000 carries an estimated five-year federal fiscal cost of $293,000,000 ($3,000,000 in 2025–2026, $70,000,000 in 2026–2027, $85,000,000 in 2027–2028, $65,000,000 in 2028–2029, and $70,000,000 in 2029–2030).

Royal Assent of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026): Introduced in the 45th Parliament, 1st Session, Bill C-15 (An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025; short title: Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 as Statutes of Canada 2026, c. 3. Enactment codified the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, ECPC eligibility, and restored capital and lease expenditure rules into the Income Tax Act effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and eligible property acquired after December 15, 2024).

body.text: 1.2 Budget 2026 Commercialization Expansion, Corporate Tax Elections, and IP Policy

Budget 2026 (published in November 2026, following the Spring Economic Update 2026) proposed a second wave of structural modernization aimed at bridging Canada's commercialization gap. For expenditures incurred in taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026, Budget 2026 proposes expanding the SR&ED tax incentive program beyond pure scientific or experimental investigation to include specific downstream commercialization expenses incurred to bring a new product or process to market—specifically costs associated with obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications, and costs for securing and maintaining intellectual property (IP) protection. To provide administrative clarity for claimants, Budget 2026 directs the CRA to publish sector-specific eligibility guidance governing commercialization outlays.

In Table 1 (Revenue Impacts of Proposed Tax Measures) of Budget 2026, the Department of Finance Canada projects that the SR&ED commercialization expansion will deliver $930,000,000 in business income tax relief over five fiscal years—comprising $25,000,000 in 2026–2027, $200,000,000 in 2027–2028, $245,000,000 in 2028–2029, $225,000,000 in 2029–2030, and $235,000,000 in 2030–2031, with $235,000,000 in ongoing annual support. Alongside commercialization eligibility, Budget 2026 proposes cutting corporate compliance red tape under its Corporate Tax Elections measure by eliminating the requirement for corporations to file a certified copy of a corporate resolution or authorization when making prescribed SR&ED agreements or elections—expressly covering transfers of qualified SR&ED expenditures and allocations of wages and salary of SR&ED employees—for elections and agreements made on or after the date of Royal Assent of the enacting legislation.

Notably, Budget 2026 did not introduce a federal "patent box" preferential tax rate on IP revenues. Instead of lowering statutory tax rates on back-end patent royalties, Ottawa elected to subsidize front-end IP registration/maintenance and regulatory certification directly through the SR&ED credit, while amending the Patent Act to require registration of patent ownership changes with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) to lower investor due-diligence risk, modernizing commercialization policies at Canada's three federal granting councils—the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC), and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR)—launching expert consultations on post-secondary technology transfer, and introducing broader scale-up incentives including the Canada Growth Incentive and enhanced Small Business Rollover. At the subnational level, Québec remains distinct in offering a dedicated patent-box-style corporate deduction—the Déduction incitative pour la commercialisation des innovations (DICI), which taxes eligible Québec IP commercialization income at 2% rather than 11.5%, according to Québec tax advisory summaries.
1.3 Federal Tax Expenditure Scale and Claimant Demographics

Data published by the Department of Finance Canada in its 2026 Report on Federal Tax Expenditures (released February 2026) underscore the macroeconomic weight of the SR&ED program. In the 2023 taxation year, approximately 23,090 corporations and 3,300 unincorporated individuals claimed SR&ED ITCs (with trust claimant counts withheld due to confidentiality rules), while roughly 18,940 corporations recorded eligible Section 37 SR&ED pool expenditures. Quantified federal SR&ED tax expenditures surpassed $5.19 billion in 2025 and are projected to reach $5.34 billion in 2026 and $5.57 billion in 2027 (with Budget 2026 Annex 1 projecting baseline SR&ED incentives to climb from $5.5 billion to $6.4 billion across its medium-term fiscal horizon).

The composition of federal tax expenditures between 2024 and 2025 illustrates the structural reallocation triggered by the post-December 15, 2024 Bill C-15 reforms: refundable corporate SR&ED ITCs surged by $470,000,000 in a single year (from $2,735,000,000 in 2024 to $3,205,000,000 in 2025, rising to $3,420,000,000 by 2027), while non-refundable corporate ITCs declined by $235,000,000 in 2025 (from $2,205,000,000 to $1,970,000,000) as scaling CCPCs and newly eligible Canadian public corporations shifted R&D outlays from the 15% non-refundable general rate into the 35% refundable enhanced rate.
2. Statutory Architecture and Eligibility of SR&ED Work
2.1 Core Statutory Framework under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal SR&ED program is codified in the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. Rather than relying on a super-deduction multiplier, the federal statute delivers two distinct, sequential tax incentives:

items: Section 37 Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool: Subsection 37(1) permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to accumulate allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, eligible SR&ED capital expenditures—incurred in Canada into a cumulative pool. Claimants may deduct any portion up to 100% against current-year income or carry unutilized pool balances forward indefinitely into future taxation years.

Sections 127 and 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC): Claimants earn a federal ITC (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) on their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" as defined in subsection 127(9), which may offset federal Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5) or generate a cash refund under section 127.1. Whenever a claimant utilizes an SR&ED ITC to reduce federal tax payable or receives an ITC cash refund, that credit amount reduces the taxpayer's pool of deductible Section 37 SR&ED expenditures in the next taxation year (tracked via Line 435 of Form T661 pursuant to Guide T4088), preventing a double tax benefit on the subsidized portion of the outlay.

body.text: 2.2 The Subsection 248(1) Definition of SR&ED and the CRA's Eligibility Methodology

Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". An eligible "SR&ED project" comprises a set of interrelated activities collectively necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements, executed by qualified personnel. Within that definition, paragraphs (a) through (d) establish three categories of eligible core research and one category of commensurate support work:

items: Basic Research (Paragraph 248(1)(a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Applied Research (Paragraph 248(1)(b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Experimental Development (Paragraph 248(1)(c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada; crucially, incremental process or product improvements qualify so long as the claimant confronts genuine technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved through routine product development or standard engineering.

Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)): Linked conjunctively ("and") to paragraphs (a), (b), and (c) following statutory amendment, paragraph (d) covers work commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development, provided the work falls within one of eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Standalone computer programming, engineering, or testing divorced from an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty does not qualify.

body.text: Under the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (issued August 13, 2021), CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) evaluate project eligibility through a structured inquiry centred on why and how the investigation was conducted. Specifically, a systematic investigation or search requires: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known scientific or technological facts as a starting point toward resolving a problem or uncertainty; (2) testing that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing proceeds); (3) developing logical conclusions grounded in experimental or analytical findings; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses. As confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), the CRA's 2021 Guidelines did not relax or remove the statutory and common-law requirement to follow the scientific method.
2.3 Statutorily Excluded Work and the Temporal Boundary for Commercialization Costs

Subsection 248(1) expressly excludes specific commercial, extractive, and non-technological activities from the definition of SR&ED: market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. Jurisprudence and administrative guidelines likewise exclude routine product development, routine marketing, and general administrative activities.

Auditors must enforce a strict fiscal-period cut-off regarding downstream commercialization outlays: for all taxation years beginning prior to Budget Day 2026, federal SR&ED claims cannot include routine regulatory certification filings or patent prosecution and IP maintenance fees. Only for expenditures incurred in taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026—pursuant to the Budget 2026 Notice of Ways and Means Motion and forthcoming sector-specific CRA guidance—will eligible regulatory approval/certification expenses and IP protection/maintenance costs enter the federal SR&ED program. By contrast, at the provincial level in Québec, regulatory validation studies and product design tied to Québec R&D already qualify under the CRIC for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Caps, Phase-Outs, and Refundability Mechanics
3.1 Basic (15%) Versus Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Tiers
Under section 127 of the Income Tax Act, federal SR&ED ITCs are calculated across two rate tiers:

items: Enhanced ITC Rate (35%): Consisting of the 15% basic credit under paragraph 127(9)(a.1) plus a 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1), the 35% enhanced rate applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the claimant's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, access was restricted exclusively to CCPCs up to a maximum expenditure limit of $3,000,000 ($1,050,000 maximum enhanced ITC). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the maximum expenditure limit to $6,000,000 ($2,100,000 maximum enhanced ITC) and extended eligibility for the 35% rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs.

Basic ITC Rate (15%): Earned under subsection 127(9) on the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool of non-CCPC / non-ECPC corporations (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries), unincorporated individuals, beneficiaries of trusts, partners of partnerships, and CCPCs or ECPCs on qualified expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit.

body.text: 3.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Outs: Taxable Capital Versus Three-Year Average Revenue

The $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit must be shared across an associated corporate group (allocated via Schedule T2SCH49) and adjusted for short taxation years. Under Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, two distinct phase-out mechanisms govern access to the $6,000,000 limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024:

items: CCPC Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000): Following Budget 2019's repeal of the prior-year taxable income phase-out for CCPCs, a CCPC's expenditure limit is phased out gradually based on taxable capital employed in Canada for the preceding taxation year. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the gradual reduction of the $6,000,000 limit begins when prior-year taxable capital reaches $15,000,000 and reduces the limit to nil at $75,000,000—expanding the phase-out span from $40,000,000 (under the pre-December 16, 2024 thresholds of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000) to $60,000,000.

ECPC Three-Year Average Annual Revenue Phase-Out (and Optional CCPC Election): Defined in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act (incorporating designated stock exchange listing rules), ECPCs do not phase out their $6,000,000 expenditure limit using taxable capital; instead, an ECPC's expenditure limit phase-out is calculated using its average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years, adjusted for short taxation years. Critically, CRA policy confirms that CCPCs may also elect via a prescribed form to compute their expenditure limit phase-out using this three-year average annual revenue method rather than prior-year taxable capital. For capital-intensive private clean-tech, semiconductor, or biotechnology CCPCs whose equity financing rounds push prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 while commercial revenues remain modest, electing the three-year revenue method preserves the full $6,000,000 enhanced limit.

body.text: 3.3 Qualifying Corporation Formulas and the Section 127.1 Cash Refundability Matrix

Under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, cash refundability of unused SR&ED ITCs (where no federal Part I tax is otherwise payable) varies sharply across both expenditure nature (current vs. capital) and claimant classification. Specifically, even when a CCPC or ECPC earns the enhanced 35% credit rate, current expenditures and PPA are refunded at 100%, whereas restored capital expenditures are refunded at 40% (leaving the remaining 60% of the 35% credit—equal to 21% of capital cost—as a non-refundable ITC carryback or carryforward).

Furthermore, for basic 15% ITCs earned by a CCPC above its $6,000,000 limit (or by an Excluded Corporation CCPC), a 40% cash refund is available only if the CCPC meets the subsection 127.1(2) definition of a "qualifying corporation"—meaning its prior-year taxable income does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. Thus, while Budget 2019 removed prior-year taxable income from the 35% expenditure limit formula, prior-year taxable income still determines whether basic 15% ITCs are 40% refundable for a CCPC. Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, the exact statutory Qualifying Income Limit formulas are:

items: For taxation years beginning BEFORE December 16, 2024: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount is ≤ $10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount of taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000.

For taxation years beginning AFTER December 15, 2024: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount of taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000.

3.4 Carrybacks, Carryforwards, Acquisition-of-Control Restrictions, and ITC Recapture

Earned SR&ED ITCs may first be applied under subsection 127(5) to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year down to nil. Any remaining current-year ITC balance that is not refunded in cash under section 127.1 may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the lesser of the undeducted current-year ITC and the prior year's Part I tax otherwise payable net of ITCs claimed or refunded in that prior year) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset future Part I tax. Availability of both carrybacks and carryforwards is subject to statutory restrictions where the corporation undergoes an acquisition of control.

Conversely, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act mandate recapture of SR&ED ITCs whenever a claimant sells or converts property from SR&ED use to commercial use (including post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital equipment, transformed materials incorporated into commercial products, or Shared-Use Equipment sold or converted all or substantially all to commercial use). The recaptured amount added back to Part I tax is determined by applying the ITC percentage originally earned on the property to the proceeds of disposition (if sold to an arm's-length person) or the fair market value of the property (in any other case, including non-arm's-length transfers or internal commercial conversion), capped at the original ITC earned.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Elections, and Restored Capital Rules
4.1 Salaries, Wages, Unpaid Remuneration, and Specified Employee YMPE Ceilings

Under subsection 248(1) and subsection 37(8) of the Income Tax Act, eligible SR&ED salary or wages comprise employment income computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I for employees directly engaged in prosecuting SR&ED in Canada. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, four strict compliance exclusions and caps govern payroll audits:

items: 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4)): Any employee remuneration (accrued salary, wages, or bonus) that is not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not incurred in that taxation year and must be excluded from allowable SR&ED expenditures.
Excluded Non-Cash Benefits and Stock Options: Neither the value of non-cash taxable benefits nor employee stock option benefits is considered an expenditure incurred for SR&ED.

GST/HST and PST Input Tax Credit Exclusion (Subsection 248(16)): Where taxable benefits reported on an employee's T4 slip include a GST/HST or provincial sales tax (PST) component for which the employer can claim an input tax credit or rebate, subsection 248(16) deems that recoverable tax to be government assistance; accordingly, no recoverable GST/HST or PST component may be included in allowable SR&ED wages.

Specified Employee Ceilings (5 × YMPE and Regulation 2900(7)): For SR&ED purposes, the maximum amount of allowable salaries and wages per specified employee (shared where a specified employee also performs SR&ED for an associated corporation) is strictly capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan. Additional restrictions govern specified employee inclusions in the Prescribed Proxy Amount salary base under Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8), which limit each specified employee's inclusion to the lesser of 75% of that employee's salary or wages for the year and 2.5 × YMPE (prorated by days of employment and shared across associated corporations), and under the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy. Auditors must ensure calculations use the first earnings ceiling (YMPE) rather than the higher CPP2 Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE). Based on official CRA Registered Plans Directorate limits through 2027, the exact full-year (365-day) specified employee salary caps are:
2025 Calendar Year: YMPE = $71,300 (vs. YAMPE of $81,200) → Maximum specified employee SR&ED salary = 5 × $71,300 = $356,500.
2026 Calendar Year: YMPE = $74,600 (vs. YAMPE of $85,000) → Maximum specified employee SR&ED salary = 5 × $74,600 = $373,000.
2027 Calendar Year: YMPE = $76,700 (vs. YAMPE of $87,400) → Maximum specified employee SR&ED salary = 5 × $76,700 = $383,500.

body.text: 4.2 Overhead Calculation Election: Proxy Method (55% PPA) Versus Traditional Method

Pursuant to subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant elects annually in Section A of Part 3 of Form T661 whether to claim SR&ED expenditures under the Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). Both methods remain subject to Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, which excludes prescribed non-R&D expenditures from the ITC base.

body.text: 4.3 Materials, Arm's-Length Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

Under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, materials consumed (rendered virtually valueless during experimentation) or materials transformed (integrated into experimental prototypes or trial runs) in performing SR&ED in Canada qualify at 100% for both Section 37 pool deduction and Section 127 ITCs, subject to subsection 127(27) ITC recapture if transformed materials are later sold or converted to commercial use.

For outsourced R&D, payments under arm's-length contracts for SR&ED directly undertaken on behalf of the claimant in Canada, as well as third-party payments to eligible research entities, are restricted to 80% ITC eligibility (reflecting Budget 2012's removal of the assumed contractor profit element) while remaining 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool. Where SR&ED is subcontracted between non-arm's-length (NAL) persons, the payer cannot claim contract payments directly as 80% qualified expenditures; instead, the NAL performer claims its underlying SR&ED costs or transfers all or part of its qualified expenditures to the payer by executing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), subject to post-December 15, 2024 NAL cost adjustments under subsection 127(11.6); where NAL parties allocate assistance, they use Form T1145, and assistance allocated to a claimant is reported on Line 540 of Form T661.
4.4 Restored SR&ED Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs

Codified by Bill C-15 and detailed in the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, capital and equipment lease outlays are governed by strict temporal and operational tests:

items: Hard December 15, 2024 Cut-Off: Depreciable property or rights to use property acquired before December 16, 2024 remain 100% ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives (including on Lines 390, 504, 535, and 540 of Form T661). Only depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024, and lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024 (for equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 in performer transfer contexts), qualify. Where a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024, SR&ED operating-time percentages must be calculated strictly over the period after December 15, 2024. Buildings, land, and leasehold interests in buildings remain excluded.

Pure SR&ED Capital Expenditures (≥90% ASA Standard): Expenditures to acquire new or used depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualify at 100% for both immediate Section 37 pool expensing and Section 127 ITCs (claimed on Line 390 of Form T661, with 40% cash refundability on 35% ITCs) if at acquisition the claimant intended either to: (1) use the property during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada; or (2) consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. Claimants must list up to the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties claimed on Line 390 on Line 262 of Form T661 and enter each property's SR&ED operating-time percentage on Line 263.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — >50% to <90% SR&ED Use): Identically under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, depreciable property that does not meet the 90% ASA threshold qualifies as first-term SUE under subsection 127(9) if it meets six cumulative conditions: (1) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024; (2) brand-new property (never used, acquired for use, or rented for any purpose prior to acquisition—used equipment cannot qualify as SUE); (3) does not qualify as a 90% ASA SR&ED capital expenditure; (4) is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (meaning the claimant must demonstrate an intention at acquisition to use the asset primarily [>50%] for SR&ED over its expected useful life); (5) is not General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF); and (6) is actually used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED in Canada during its operating time in the first period (ending at the close of the first taxation year occurring at least 12 months after acquisition). Continued primary (>50%) SR&ED use through the second period qualifies the asset as second-term SUE. SUE capital cost does not enter the Section 37 SR&ED pool and is instead depreciated via regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) on Schedule T2SCH8. On Form T661 Line 504, the claimant claims 25% (1/4) of the capital cost in the first period and another 25% (1/4) in the second period (computed excluding Section 21 borrowed money and deemed capital cost rules, and after subsection 127(11.6) NAL adjustments), subject to ITC recapture upon sale or ASA conversion to commercial use.

body.text: 4.5 Cloud Computing, Software Costs, and AI Hardware Infrastructure

While the CRA's published SR&ED policies do not isolate a separate cloud-computing administrative circular, the statutory boundary between service overheads and depreciable capital property in the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations establishes clear treatment for cloud, software, and AI compute costs:

items: On-Demand Cloud Compute and R&D Software Subscriptions: Metered cloud computing instances and software development tools do not involve acquiring depreciable property. Under the Proxy Method, such service outlays are treated as overhead subsumed within the notional 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately. Under the Traditional Method, cloud compute and R&D software costs that are directly related and incremental to prosecuting SR&ED or providing SR&ED computing facilities (and carefully segregated from commercial production hosting) are claimable as overhead on Line 360 under paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b) (alongside eligible technical training costs referenced in the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy).

Owned On-Premise Compute Servers: Dedicated R&D compute clusters or specialized laboratory hardware (other than GPOEF) acquired after December 15, 2024 qualify for 100% immediate expensing and 100% ITC inclusion if meeting the ≥90% ASA test, or 25% + 25% SUE ITCs (plus regular CCA) if purchased brand-new and used primarily (>50% to <90%) in SR&ED. (In Québec, computer hardware and management software may alternatively qualify for the refundable 15%/20%/25% C3i credit, and AI integration salaries qualify under the post-2025 CDAEIA credit, though Québec prohibits double-claiming C3i and CRIC on the same expense, according to Québec tax advisory guides).

body.text: 5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Alignment Analysis

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer subnational R&D tax credits, whereas Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut provide no provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Following Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, subnational alignment across Canada diverged markedly between followers and structural holdouts.
5.1 Québec's CRIC Overhaul and Specialized Innovation Credits (DICI, CDAEIA, C3i)

Administered independently by Revenu Québec, Québec enacted a comprehensive modernization of its R&D tax architecture for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025. Official Gouvernement du Québec and Revenu Québec publications confirm that previous Québec R&D credits—including the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V; formerly 14% base / 30% enhanced per advisory summaries), the University/Public Research Centre Credit (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research Credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Research Consortium Fees/Dues Credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, whose cumulative balance at the end of a period ending after March 25, 2025 remains claimable for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029)—were replaced by the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (consolidated across eight prior measures pursuant to Québec Finance Bulletin 2025-6, according to Québec advisory guides).
Official Gouvernement du Québec CRIC rules establish the following parameters:

items: Eligible Claimants & Filing: Available strictly to corporations (and corporate members of partnerships) operating a business in Québec with an establishment in Québec, claimed via Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (with Form RD-222-V for R&D deductions; individuals, trusts, specified partnership members, and corporations holding a Large Investment Project tax holiday certificate on the same property are ineligible).

Dual Activity Scope (R&D + Pre-Commercialization): Covers both traditional R&D (basic research, applied research, and experimental development harmonized with federal subsection 248(1)) AND pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with Québec R&D—specifically: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; and (2) product design, including development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials.

Qualified Expenditures: Comprises 100% of salaries or wages paid to employees for eligible Québec R&D or pre-commercialization; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec; 50% of payments to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and 100% of eligible depreciable property acquisition costs (excluding buildings, land, or rights to use a building or land).

Applicable Exclusion Threshold: Qualified expenditures in the taxation year must exceed the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Basic Personal Amount (BPA) under the Québec personal income tax system for each employee, prorated by the time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities (Québec R&D tax advisory firms report the Québec BPA at $18,952 per FTE for 2026, up from approximately $18,571 in 2025).

Refundable Credit Rates: Provides a 100% refundable corporate tax credit of 30% on qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold up to a maximum band of $1,000,000, and 20% on qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 band.

body.text: In addition to CRIC (which cannot be stacked with another Québec credit on the identical expense), Québec R&D tax advisory summaries verify three parallel provincial incentives active in 2026: (1) the DICI (Déduction incitative pour la commercialisation des innovations), taxing qualifying Québec IP commercialization income at 2% instead of the 11.5% general corporate rate; (2) the CDAEIA, which replaced the legacy CDAE e-business salary credit for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025, providing a 30% credit (22% refundable + 8% non-refundable in 2026; 21% + 9% in 2027; 20% + 10% from 2028) on eligible salaries above an exclusion threshold for corporations integrating artificial intelligence features in a significant way (requiring an annual Investissement Québec certificate); and (3) the 100% refundable C3i (Crédit d'impôt pour investissement et innovation) providing 15%, 20%, or 25% by region on manufacturing/processing equipment, computer hardware, and management software above $5,000 or $12,500 per asset up to a $100,000,000 four-year cap.
5.2 Ontario's Tripartite Corporate Regime: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Administered by the CRA on behalf of Ontario under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), Ontario maintains three distinct corporate R&D credits. Specialist Canadian R&D tax advisory analysis published in October 2026 confirms that Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ECPC refundability, or restored federal capital expenditure base for its refundable credit:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC): An 8% refundable credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; claimed via Schedule T2SCH566) on up to $3,000,000 of qualifying current Ontario SR&ED expenditures ($240,000 maximum credit, shared among associated corporations). The $3,000,000 limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000, OR when prior-year specified paid-up capital lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC): A 3.5% non-refundable credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; claimed via Schedule T2SCH508) on eligible Ontario expenditures, with unused credits eligible for 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward according to provincial SR&ED advisory summaries.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97): A 20% fully refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of annual qualified current SR&ED expenditures ($4,000,000 maximum annual credit, allocated across associated corporations) incurred under an eligible contract (entered into after May 6, 1997) with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) in Ontario—including Ontario universities, community colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and Networks of Centres of Excellence—provided the corporation is not connected to the ERI (via >10% voting or fair-market-value share ownership, partnership membership, or non-arm's-length dealing). Claimed on Schedules T2SCH568 and T2SCH569 (and Line 470 of Schedule 5).

body.text: 5.3 Western, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes: Followers Versus Independent Holdouts
Across Western, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, CRA official guides and October 2026 provincial SR&ED advisory reviews establish the following alignment landscape:

items: British Columbia (Full Federal Alignment & Permanent Status): Administered by the CRA via Form T666 at a 10% credit rate (refundable for qualifying CCPCs up to the expenditure limit and non-refundable on excess or non-qualifying corporate spend). While the CRA's general provincial summary reflects the historical $3,000,000 CCPC limit ($300,000 refundable maximum), October 2026 Canadian R&D tax advisory analysis reports that British Columbia expressly aligned with all principal Bill C-15 federal changes for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—increasing B.C.'s refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 ($600,000 maximum refund), adopting the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, extending refundable access to ECPCs, restoring capital expenditures, and repealing the credit's sunset date in B.C. Budget 2026 to make the B.C. SR&ED credit permanent.

Alberta (Independent Innovation Employment Grant — IEG): Administered directly by the Province of Alberta (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970; guidance updated June 30, 2026 per advisory tracking), Alberta retained its independent structure capped at $4,000,000 of annual eligible Alberta R&D spending, providing an 8% refundable payment up to the corporation's two-year average historical Alberta R&D base and a 20% refundable payment (8% base + 12% incremental) on eligible spending above that base.

Saskatchewan (Province-Specific CCPC Expansion): Administered by the CRA (Form T2SCH403) at a 10% rate. While CRA baseline summaries note the post-April 1, 2017 $1,000,000 refundable CCPC cap, October 2026 specialist tax advisory analysis reports that for expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled its 10% refundable CCPC threshold to the first $2,000,000 of annual qualifying expenditures (10% non-refundable above $2,000,000 and for non-CCPCs, subject to a $1,000,000 combined annual credit cap per corporation), without adopting the $6,000,000 limit or ECPC access.

Manitoba: Administered by the CRA (Form T2SCH380), providing a 15% credit on eligible expenditures (including provincial depreciable capital excluding buildings/leasehold interests)—100% refundable under contract with a qualifying institute, and 50% refundable (7.5%) / 50% non-refundable (7.5%) for in-house R&D, without using the federal expenditure limit.

Atlantic Provinces & Yukon: Administered by the CRA, Nova Scotia (Form T2SCH340), New Brunswick (Form T2SCH360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Form T2SCH301 for corporations; Form T1129 for individuals) each provide an uncapped 15% fully refundable R&D credit, while Yukon provides a 15% refundable credit plus an additional 5% refundable top-up (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: 6. Direct Federal R&D Grants, Institutional Transitions, and Stacking Mechanics
6.1 NRC IRAP, SDTC Absorption, and the Canada Innovation Corporation Timeline

Canadian innovators routinely pair retroactive SR&ED tax credits with upfront direct contribution programs administered under the mandates of Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) and the National Research Council of Canada (NRC):

items: NRC Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP): Delivers technical and business advisory services through a cross-Canada network of field professional staff alongside cost-shared, merit-based non-repayable contributions supporting SME R&D projects and post-secondary graduate employment. Under the NRC's 2025–26 Departmental Plan, NRC IRAP formally encompassed federal sustainable development technology programming following the transition of Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) into the NRC. Meanwhile, although Budget 2022 and a February 15, 2023 blueprint announced plans to transfer NRC IRAP into the Canada Innovation Corporation (CIC), official NRC and ISED departmental plans confirm that the establishment and launch of the CIC was set for 2026–2027, leaving NRC IRAP operating within the NRC pending transition.

Replacement of the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) by the Strategic Response Fund (SRF): Official ISED 2026–27 Departmental Plan tables verify that following the non-renewal of certain envelopes in the Global Innovation Clusters and SIF's Net Zero Accelerator, the Strategic Response Fund (SRF) replaced the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) with an expanded mandate. Active throughout 2025 and 2026, SRF Business Innovation and Growth contributions fund large-scale industrial R&D and commercialization centres across battery manufacturing, bioprinted tissue therapeutics, critical minerals processing, clean grid equipment, and digital/5G infrastructure.

Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC): Managed jointly by ISED and NRC IRAP, ISC issues government priority challenges and awards grants or procurement contracts to Canadian SMEs from proof-of-feasibility through prototype development.

body.text: 6.2 Worked Stacking Audit Models: Government Assistance and Current vs. Capital Cash Flow

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, direct R&D grants (such as NRC IRAP) and provincial R&D tax credits (such as Québec's CRIC or Ontario's OITC) constitute government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool prior to computing the 35% or 15% federal ITC. Two numerical audit models illustrate how multi-jurisdictional stacking and post-December 15, 2024 capital refundability rules operate in 2026:

items: Audit Model A — 2026 Québec CCPC Stacking CRIC + Federal 35% SR&ED (Proxy Method): Consider a Québec CCPC (taxation year January 1 to December 31, 2026; prior-year taxable capital below $15,000,000) paying $1,200,000 in salaries to 5 full-time arm's-length R&D engineers in Québec and $200,000 to an arm's-length Québec R&D subcontractor ($1,400,000 cash spend). For Québec CRIC, eligible expenditures equal $1,200,000 (100% wages) + $100,000 (50% of $200,000 subcontract) = $1,300,000. Subtracting the 2026 employee BPA exclusion threshold reported by Québec R&D advisors (5 × $18,952 = $94,760, exceeding the $50,000 minimum floor) leaves $1,205,240 above the threshold, generating $300,000 (30% on the first $1,000,000) plus $41,048 (20% on the excess $205,240) = $341,048 in refundable CRIC. (Using an illustrative rounded $100,000 threshold, as modelled in Québec R&D advisory literature, yields $340,000 CRIC). For Federal SR&ED, gross Proxy Method QREs equal $1,200,000 (100% wages) + $660,000 (55% PPA on $1,200,000 wages) + $160,000 (80% of $200,000 subcontract) = $2,020,000. Deducting the $341,048 CRIC as government assistance leaves $1,678,952 in net federal QREs, generating a 35% refundable federal ITC of $587,633.20. Combined refundable cash recovery reaches $928,681.20—offsetting 66.33% of the corporation's $1,400,000 cash outlay.

Audit Model B — 2026 ECPC or CCPC Cash-Flow Split Across Current, ASA Capital, and Shared-Use Equipment: Consider an ECPC or CCPC with zero Part I tax payable in 2026 (within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, Proxy Method) incurring $1,000,000 in directly engaged R&D salaries, $1,000,000 on a dedicated ASA (≥90% SR&ED) laboratory asset acquired in 2026, and $800,000 on brand-new Shared-Use Equipment used primarily (>50% to <90%) in SR&ED across Period 1 and Period 2. First, the $1,000,000 current wages plus $550,000 (55% PPA) = $1,550,000 current QREs earn $542,500 in gross 35% ITC, paid out at 100% cash refundability ($542,500 immediate cash). Second, the $1,000,000 ASA capital asset is 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and earns $350,000 in gross 35% ITC, but under Section 127.1 capital ITCs are 40% cash refundable—delivering $140,000 in immediate cash (40% × $350,000) and $210,000 as a non-refundable ITC carryback/carryforward. Third, the $800,000 SUE asset is depreciated under regular Schedule T2SCH8 CCA while claiming 25% ($200,000) on Form T661 Line 504 in Period 1 and 25% ($200,000) in Period 2—generating $70,000 gross 35% ITC per period, split into $28,000 immediate cash (40% × $70,000) and $42,000 non-refundable carryforward in each of Period 1 and Period 2.

body.text: 7. Governing Authorities, Filing Deadlines, 2026 Form Updates, and Audit Procedures
7.1 Prescribed Forms, 2026 Form T661 Line Additions, and the Strict 12-Month Reporting Deadline

Under the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, a claimant's SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year. Expenditures must be entered on the appropriate lines of Form T661 alongside Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals) on or before that statutory reporting deadline; failure to file prescribed forms and project information on time results in mandatory disallowance of the unclaimed SR&ED expenditures. Once expenditures have been timely reported into the Section 37 deductible pool on Form T661, however, drawing down deductions from that pool in subsequent years is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline.

body.text: In Part 2 of Form T661 (Project Information, Sections A to C), claimants must adhere to strict word limits and chronological technical prompts prepared by personnel familiar with the scientific or technical work (reporting start and completion dates on Lines 203 and 204). Claimants with numerous projects may submit Part 2 descriptions at initial filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided Part 6 includes the costs of every claimed project and complete Part 2 forms for all claimed projects are maintained at the claimant's place of business for immediate submission upon CRA request.
7.2 Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026), Processing Capacity, and Audit Outcomes

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process via My Business Account, enabling eligible businesses to determine whether planned projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before starting work or incurring expenditures. The CRA issues a formal determination within eight weeks of application submission, supported by one-on-one outreach sessions, upgraded SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) interfaces, and revised review procedures in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants. Concurrently, targeted administrative investments announced in the Spring Economic Update 2026 were projected to expand CRA claim-processing throughput more than 4.5-fold by July 2026 to clear claim backlogs, while historical CRA guidance for SR&ED claims by physicians and medical professional corporations was formally archived in 2026.

When a filed claim undergoes joint compliance review by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR) under the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, the resulting SR&ED Review Report (SRR) records one of five project outcomes: AW (all reviewed work meets subsection 248(1)), SW (some reviewed work meets subsection 248(1) and some does not), NW (no claimed work meets subsection 248(1)), UN (unsubstantiated—insufficient evidence to determine whether claimed work meets subsection 248(1)), or AAF (accepted as filed without technical review, which neither confirms nor refutes eligibility). Separate from project disallowance, Part 9 of Form T661 mandates full disclosure of any external claim preparer accepting consideration and their billing arrangement: while Part 9 is not subject to the 12-month disallowance deadline and errors do not invalidate the SR&ED claim itself, missing, incomplete, or inaccurate Part 9 information triggers a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable.
8. Judicial Precedents and Litigated Standards in Canadian SR&ED Law
8.1 The Northwest Hydraulic Five-Criteria Test and Appellate Endorsement in C.W. Agencies

Canadian courts interpret subsection 248(1) through the landmark five-criteria legal framework articulated by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC) and unanimously endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal (Stone, Evans, and Sexton JJ.A., per Sexton J.A.) in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada), 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA). Together with RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canada, 2011 FCA 355 (aff'g 2011 TCC 261), and Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (per Justice Sommerfeldt), Canadian jurisprudence enforces five cumulative requirements:

items: Technological Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? As emphasized in Jentel, SR&ED tax benefits are granted in addition to ordinary business deductions specifically to subsidize overcoming technological uncertainty to achieve technological advancement—never to subsidize routine product development.
Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the claimant formulate clear hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

Systematic Investigation Following the Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with the discipline of the scientific method—testing and modifying hypotheses through systematic experiment or analysis?
Technological Advancement: Did the process seek or yield a technological advancement?
Contemporaneous Documentation: Were records of the hypotheses tested and results obtained generated and kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 8.2 Statutory Interpretation, Software Claims, and Expert Evidence in Kam-Press and National R&D
Two modern Federal Court of Appeal rulings govern current CRA technical reviews and Tax Court litigation, particularly in software engineering and applied technology disputes:

items: Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (FCA): Reaffirmed that it is strictly the role of the courts—not administrative agency guidelines—to interpret and elaborate upon the statutory meaning of Income Tax Act provisions.

National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47): Affirming the dismissal of a software development SR&ED appeal in which technological uncertainty existed at the outset but the remaining Northwest Hydraulic criteria were unmet, the Federal Court of Appeal established three crucial principles. First, echoing Kam-Press, the Court held that the CRA's simplified August 2021 SR&ED eligibility guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method. Second, the Court confirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic test applies in a flexible manner suitable for applied sciences while accounting for the taxpayer's business environment, yet still requires systematic hypothesis testing and analysis rather than unrecorded coding iteration. Third, affirming the exclusion of the taxpayer's expert witness report, the FCA warned litigants against submitting expert opinions that opine directly on the ultimate legal question of whether claimed work constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1).

body.text: 9. Strategic Compliance and Audit Verification Checklist

items: Apply Enacted Post-December 15, 2024 Thresholds and Screen ECPC / Revenue Elections: Verify that taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 apply the enacted $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit and $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital corridor under Bill C-15 (never the superseded $4,500,000 FES 2024 proposal), screen Canadian public corporations for newly enacted ECPC 35% refundability, and test whether high-capital CCPCs benefit from electing the three-year average annual revenue phase-out method.

Audit Capital Acquisition Dates, Brand-New SUE Status, and 40% Cash Refundability: Confirm every claimed SR&ED capital or SUE asset was acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, verify SUE items are brand-new, non-PDP, and non-GPOEF, complete Lines 262, 263, and 504 on Form T661, and model 40% cash refundability (not 100%) on 35% capital ITCs.

Enforce Specified Employee YMPE Caps and the 180-Day Payment Rule: Verify all accrued wages were paid within 180 days of fiscal year-end under subsection 78(4), strip out non-cash benefits, stock options, and recoverable GST/HST/PST, and cap specified employee wages using the exact YMPE ($71,300 in 2025; $74,600 in 2026; $76,700 in 2027) rather than YAMPE.

Compare Proxy (55% PPA) Versus Traditional Overhead Before Filing: Model whether incremental cloud compute, R&D software, facility overheads, and <90% post-December 15, 2024 equipment leases on Line 360 under the Traditional Method outperform the notional 55% PPA before making the annual subsection 37(10) election.

Align Multi-Provincial Filings (Québec CRIC, B.C. Permanency, Ontario Caps): Transition Québec taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 to Form RD-1029.8.CR-T to capture 30%/20% CRIC on both R&D and Québec pre-commercialization activities (and transition CDAE to CDAEIA after December 31, 2025), claim harmonized $6,000,000 limits in British Columbia, and retain the $3,000,000 OITC cap in Ontario.

Segregate Pre- vs. Post-Budget 2026 Commercialization Expenses: Exclude regulatory approval/certification and IP protection costs from federal SR&ED claims for taxation years beginning before Budget Day 2026, while establishing dedicated general-ledger tracking for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026.

Sequence Government Assistance Accurately on Proxy Claims: Compute the 55% PPA on eligible directly engaged wages in Part 5 of Form T661 before deducting NRC IRAP, SRF contributions, and provincial R&D tax credits (CRIC, OITC, B.C. SR&ED, IEG) as government assistance in Part 4.

Maintain Contemporaneous Hypothesis-Driven Evidence: Pursuant to Northwest Hydraulic and National R&D, ensure engineering tickets, code repositories, bench logs, and failure analyses document hypotheses, systematic tests, and conclusions as the work progresses.

Verify 2026 Form T661 Mandatory Codes, Pre-Claim Numbers, and Part 9 Disclosures: Enter the 5-digit Statistics Canada CRDC 2020 v2.0 RDF##### code on Line 207, record any April 2026 Pre-Claim Approval case number on Lines 212/214, and audit Part 9 preparer fee disclosures to avoid the $1,000 joint-and-several/solidary penalty.

Lock Calendar Controls Ahead of the 12-Month Post-Filing-Due-Date Cliff: Enforce strict internal sign-off well ahead of the unwaivable statutory SR&ED reporting deadline (12 months after the income tax return filing due date).
